studies.title: The Additive Effects of Creatine Supplementation and Exercise Training in an Aging Population: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
studies.abstract: The role of creatine supplementation in young athletes and bodybuilders is well established including ergogenic properties of muscular hypertrophy, strength, power, and endurance. Whether the benefits of creatine supplementation translate to an aging population with moderate training stimulus remains unclear especially in regard to gender, creatine dose, and duration. This systematic review assessed whether creatine supplementation combined with exercise results in additive improvements in indices of skeletal muscle, bone, and mental health over exercise alone in healthy older adults. PubMed, CINAHL, and Web of Science databases were utilized to identify randomized controlled trials of creatine supplementation combined with exercise in an aging population with additional predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts, reviewed full-text articles, and performed quality assessments using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale. Seventeen studies were comprehensively reviewed according to categories of strength, endurance, functional capacity, body composition, cognition, and safety. These studies suggest that any additive ergogenic creatine effects on upper and/or lower body strength, functional capacity, and lean mass in an older population would require a continuous and daily low-dose creatine supplementation combined with at least 12 weeks of resistance training. Potential creatine specific increases in regional bone mineral density of the femur are possible but may require at least 1 year of creatine supplementation combined with moderate resistance training, and additional long-term clinical trials are warranted. The limited data suggested no additive effects of creatine over exercise alone on indices of mental health. The beneficial effects of creatine supplementation are more consistent in older women than in men. Creatine monohydrate is safe to use in older adults. While creatine in conjunction with moderate- to high-intensity exercise in an aging population may improve skeletal muscle health, additional studies are needed to determine the effective dosing and duration paradigm for potential combined creatine and exercise effects on bone and cognition in older adults.

studies.title: Effect of creatine monohydrate on motor function in children with facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy: A multicenter, randomized, double-blind placebo-contro
studies.abstract:
Background

Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is a rare, progressive muscle disease with no available disease-modifying therapy. Creatine monohydrate (CrM) has been shown to improve muscle strength in individuals with muscular dystrophies but has not been tested in young people with FSHD. This study aimed to explore the efficacy of CrM on motor function in children with FSHD.

Methods

In a randomized placebo-controlled double-blind crossover trial, powdered CrM at a dose of 100 mg/kg/day (maximum 10 g daily) was compared with placebo in two 12-week treatment periods with a 6-week washout between crossover arms. The primary outcome measure was the Motor Function Measure for Neuromuscular Disease (MFM-32) with secondary outcomes assessing safety, endurance, strength, patient-reported outcome measures, and muscle morphology measurements as assessed by whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Results

Thirteen children were enrolled (mean (standard deviation, SD) 12.2 (2.67) years of age) and 11 patients completed both trial treatment periods. In an intention-to-treat analysis, no clinically meaningful difference was seen between treatment groups as measured by the mean difference in MFM-32 (0.19, 95% confidence interval (CI) -0.71 to 1.08). However, there was an improvement in 6-minute walk distance of 27.74 m (95% CI -1.41 to 56.88) and trends to improvement in the FSHD-Composite Outcome Measure for Pediatrics (FSHD-COM Peds), 10 meter walk/run, and in MRI measures. There were no serious adverse events. Serum creatinine increased by a mean 12.63 μmol/L (95% CI 1.14 to 24.12) post-CrM treatment, though this was presumed to reflect increased creatinine production. No participants discontinued CrM due to adverse events.

Conclusion

CrM is safe and well tolerated in children with FSHD. Although CrM had no effect on motor function as measured by the MFM-32 compared with placebo, there were trends toward improvement in the 6-minute walk distance and other secondary outcome measures. This study confirms the feasibility of conducting clinical trials in children with FSHD. Further assessment of the efficacy of CrM in pediatric FSHD is warranted in a larger randomized controlled clinical trial. Future studies may benefit from stratifying population cohorts according to functional ability or by MRI fat infiltration measurements.

studies.title: Short term creatine loading improves strength endurance even without changing maximal strength, RPE, fatigue index, blood lactate, and mode state.
studies.abstract: Creatine is consumed by athletes to increase strength and gain muscle. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of creatine supplementation on maximal strength and strength endurance. Twelve strength-trained men (25.2 ± 3.4 years) supplemented with 20 g Creatina + 10g maltodextrin or placebo (20g starch + 10g maltodextrin) for five days in randomized order. Maximal strength and strength endurance (4 sets 70% 1RM until concentric failure) were determined in the bench press. In addition, blood lactate, rate of perceived effort, fatigue index, and mood state were evaluated. All measurements were performed before and after the supplementation period. There were no significant changing in maximal strength, blood lactate, RPE, fatigue index, and mood state in either treatment. However, the creatine group performed more repetitions after the supplementation (Cr: Δ = +3.4 reps, p = 0.036, g = 0.53; PLA: Δ = +0.3reps, p = 0.414, g = 0.06), and higher total work (Cr: Δ = +199.5au, p = 0.038, g = 0.52; PLA: Δ = +26.7au, p = 0.402, g = 0.07). Creatine loading for five days allowed the subjects to perform more repetitions, resulting in greater total work, but failed to change the maximum strength.

studies.title: Effects of creatine monohydrate timing on resistance training adaptations and body composition after 8 weeks in male and female collegiate athletes.
studies.abstract:
Background

Limited research is available on the potential impact of creatine monohydrate administration before or after workouts among athletes. This study aimed to investigate the effects of pre- vs. post-exercise creatine monohydrate supplementation on resistance training adaptations and body composition.

Methods

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel design, 34 healthy resistance-trained male and female athletes were randomly assigned and matched according to fat free mass to consume a placebo, or 5-g dose of creatine monohydrate within 1 h before training, or within 1 h after training for 8 weeks, while completing a weekly resistance training program. Participants co-ingested 25-gram doses of both whey protein isolate and maltodextrin along with each assigned supplement dose. Body composition, muscular strength, and endurance, along with isometric mid-thigh pull were assessed before and after the 8-week supplementation period. A 3 × 2 mixed factorial (group x time) ANOVA with repeated measures on time were used to evaluate differences.

Results

All groups experienced similar and statistically significant increases in fat free mass (+1.34 ± 3.48 kg, p = 0.04), upper (+2.21 ± 5.69 kg, p = 0.04) and lower body strength (+7.32 ± 10.01 kg, p < 0.001), and decreases in body mass (-1.09 ± 2.71 kg, p = 0.03), fat mass (-2.64 ± 4.16 kg, p = 0.001), and percent body fat (-2.85 ± 4.39 kg, p < 0.001).

Conclusions

The timing of creatine monohydrate did not exert any additional influence over the measured outcomes.

studies.title: Effect of creatine supplementation and drop-set resistance training in untrained aging adults.
studies.abstract: To investigate the effects of creatine supplementation and drop-set resistance training in untrained aging adults. Participants were randomized to one of two groups: Creatine (CR: n=14, 7 females, 7 males; 58.0±3.0yrs, 0.1g/kg/day of creatine+0.1g/kg/day of maltodextrin) or Placebo (PLA: n=17, 7 females, 10 males; age: 57.6±5.0yrs, 0.2g/kg/day of maltodextrin) during 12weeks of drop-set resistance training (3days/week; 2 sets of leg press, chest press, hack squat and lat pull-down exercises performed to muscle fatigue at 80% baseline 1-repetition maximum [1-RM] immediately followed by repetitions to muscle fatigue at 30% baseline 1-RM). Prior to and following training and supplementation, assessments were made for body composition, muscle strength, muscle endurance, tasks of functionality, muscle protein catabolism and diet. Drop-set resistance training improved muscle mass, muscle strength, muscle endurance and tasks of functionality (p<0.05). The addition of creatine to drop-set resistance training significantly increased body mass (p=0.002) and muscle mass (p=0.007) compared to placebo. Males on creatine increased muscle strength (lat pull-down only) to a greater extent than females on creatine (p=0.005). Creatine enabled males to resistance train at a greater capacity over time compared to males on placebo (p=0.049) and females on creatine (p=0.012). Males on creatine (p=0.019) and females on placebo (p=0.014) decreased 3-MH compared to females on creatine. The addition of creatine to drop-set resistance training augments the gains in muscle mass from resistance training alone. Creatine is more effective in untrained aging males compared to untrained aging females.

studies.title: Effects of creatine monohydrate supplementation on simulated soccer performance.
studies.abstract: To determine the effects of acute short-term creatine (Cr) supplementation on physical performance during a 90-min soccer-specific performance test. A double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental design was adopted during which 16 male amateur soccer players were required to consume 20 g/d Cr for 7 d or a placebo. A Ball-Sport Endurance and Speed Test (BEAST) comprising measures of aerobic (circuit time), speed (12- and 20-m sprint), and explosive-power (vertical jump) abilities performed over 90 min was performed presupplementation and postsupplementation. Performance measures during the BEAST deteriorated during the second half relative to the first for both Cr (1.2-2.3%) and placebo (1.0-2.2%) groups, indicating a fatigue effect associated with the BEAST. However, no significant differences existed between groups, suggesting that Cr had no performance-enhancing effect or ability to offset fatigue. When effect sizes were considered, some measures (12-m sprint, -0.53 ± 0.69; 20-m sprint, -0.39 ± 0.59) showed a negative tendency, indicating chances of harm were greater than chances of benefit. Acute short-term Cr supplementation has no beneficial effect on physical measures obtained during a 90-min soccer-simulation test, thus bringing into question its potential as an effective ergogenic aid for soccer players.

studies.title: Effects of creatine supplementation on muscle power, endurance, and sprint performance.
studies.abstract: To determine the effects of creatine (Cr) supplementation (20 g x d(-1) during 5 d) on maximal strength, muscle power production during repetitive high-power-output exercise bouts (MRPB), repeated running sprints, and endurance in handball players. Nineteen trained male handball players were randomly assigned in a double-blind fashion to either creatine (N = 9) or placebo (N = 10) group. Before and after supplementation, subjects performed one-repetition maximum half-squat (1RM(HS) and bench press (1RM(BP)), 2 sets of MRPB consisting of one set of 10 continuous repetitions (R10) followed by 1 set until exhaustion (R(max)), with exactly 2-min rest periods between each set, during bench-press and half-squat protocols with a resistance equal to 60 and 70% of the subjects' 1RM, respectively. In addition, a countermovement jumping test (CMJ) interspersed before and after the MRPB half-squat exercise bouts and a repeated sprint running test and a maximal multistage discontinuous incremental running test (MDRT) were performed. Cr supplementation significantly increased body mass (from 79.4 +/- 8 to 80 +/- 8 kg; P < 0.05), number of repetitions performed to fatigue, and total average power output values in the R(max) set of MRPB during bench press (21% and 17%, respectively) and half-squat (33% and 20%, respectively), the 1RM(HS) (11%), as well as the CMJ values after the MRPB half-squat (5%), and the average running times during the first 5 m of the six repeated 15-m sprints (3%). No changes were observed in the strength, running velocity, or body mass measures in the placebo group during the experimental period. Short-term Cr supplementation leads to significant improvements in lower-body maximal strength, maximal repetitive upper- and lower-body high-power exercise bouts, and total repetitions performed to fatigue in the R(max) set of MRPB, as well as enhanced repeated sprint performance and attenuated decline in jumping ability after MRPB in highly trained handball players. Cr supplementation did not result in any improvement in upper-body maximal strength and in endurance running performance.

studies.title: Creatine therapy in myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease): a placebo-controlled crossover trial.
studies.abstract: To determine whether treatment with creatine can improve exercise intolerance in myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease). Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study with oral creatine monohydrate supplementation. Nine patients with biochemically and genetically proven McArdle disease were treated. Five days of daily high-dose creatine intake (150 mg/kg body weight) were followed by daily low-dose creatine intake (60 mg/kg). Each treatment phase with creatine or placebo lasted 5 weeks. The effect of treatment was estimated at the end of each treatment phase by recording clinical scores, ergometer exercise test results, phosphorus 31 nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and surface electromyography. Of 9 patients, 5 reported improvement of muscle complaints with creatine. Force-time integrals (P =.03) and depletion of phosphocreatine (P =.04) increased significantly during ischemic exercise with creatine. Phosphocreatine depletion also increased significantly during aerobic exercise (P =.006). The decrease of median frequency in surface electromyograms during contraction was significantly larger (P =.03) with creatine. This is the first controlled study indicating that creatine supplementation improves skeletal muscle function in McArdle disease.

studies.title: A randomized, controlled trial of creatine monohydrate in patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.
studies.abstract: Fatigue in patients with mitochondrial cytopathies is associated with decreased basal and postactivity muscle phosphocreatine (PCr). Creatine monohydrate supplementation has been shown to increase muscle PCr and high-intensity power output in healthy subjects. We studied the effects of creatine monohydrate administration (5 g PO b.i.d. x 14 days --> 2 g PO b.i.d. x 7 days) in 7 mitochondrial cytopathy patients using a randomized, crossover design. Measurements included: activities of daily living (visual analog scale); ischemic isometric handgrip strength (1 min); basal and postischemic exercise lactate; evoked and voluntary contraction strength of the dorsiflexors; nonischemic, isometric, dorsiflexion torque (NIDFT, 2 min); and aerobic cycle ergometry with pre- and post-lactate measurements. Creatine treatment resulted in significantly (P < 0.05) increased handgrip strength, NIDFT, and postexercise lactate, with no changes in the other measured variables. We concluded that creatine monohydrate increased the strength of high-intensity anaerobic and aerobic type activities in patients with mitochondrial cytopathies but had no apparent effects upon lower intensity aerobic activities.

studies.title: The effect of creatine monohydrate supplementation on obstacle course and multiple bench press performance.
studies.abstract: Dietary creatine (Cr) supplementation has been shown to enhance muscular strength and endurance. This study determined the effects of Cr supplementation on performance of military training tasks. Two groups (Cr and placebo [Pl]) of 13 male soldiers each performed 3 consecutive military obstacle course runs ( approximately 3 minutes over 7 obstacles with a 2-minute rest between runs) followed by a rifle marksmanship task on 3 occasions (T(1), T(2), and T(3)), each separated by 5 days. They also completed a bench press protocol (5 sets to failure at 70% of 1 repetition maximum) and answered the Profile of Mood States questionnaire during each test session. Testing was done 3 times. No supplementation was given before T(1). Supplementation was provided using sports bars, with both groups receiving Pl bars between T(1) and T(2), whereas from T(2) to T(3) the Cr group consumed 24 g per day of Cr monohydrate in sports bars and the Pl group consumed an equal amount (kilocalories) of Pl sports bars. Creatine usage resulted in a significant (14%) increase in total bench press repetitions (p </= 0.05), but no difference between groups in obstacle course run times for the 3 runs from T(2) to T(3). Marksmanship or mood was not affected by Cr supplementation. An increase of 1.4 kg in body mass (p </= 0.005) and a 0.5% decrease in percent body fat (p </= 0.05) were observed after Cr ingestion. Creatine supplementation over 5 days improved performance during a controlled strength test but did not significantly improve military obstacle course performance.

studies.title: Creatine Monohydrate as an Effective Supplement for Muscular Fatigue in an Ehlers-Danlos Patient.
studies.abstract: Patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) frequently report symptoms such as chronic pain and muscular fatigue that can heavily impact their quality of life. The treatment for many of the physical symptoms of EDS is focused on supportive care, which may include physical therapy and exercise programs. However, many patients will experience difficulty in deriving benefits from these activities due to significant pain and fatigue from physical activity. We report a case of a 39-year-old female with a history of EDS whose physical capabilities were severely impacted by their chronic pain and fatigue symptoms. After little progress was made with their current treatment plan of analgesics, manual therapy, exercise, and physical therapy, the patient was supplemented with creatine monohydrate due to its studied benefits in muscular strength and endurance for athletes. Following supplementation, the patient reported significant benefits in their muscular fatigue symptoms, allowing them to engage in daily activities and exercises more effectively. This case demonstrates a potential addition to the treatment of EDS that can improve a patient's quality of life.

studies.title: Supplementation of Creatine Monohydrate Improves Sprint Performance but Has no Effect on Glycolytic Contribution: A Nonrandomized, Placebo-Controlled Crossover
studies.abstract:
Background

Sprint performance may be crucial for athletes in sprint and endurance sports. In this regard, the maximal glycolytic rate (νLamax) is a variable within Mader's model of metabolism that is commonly tested in a 15-s all-out sprint test. The product of lactate accumulation (ΔLa) and lactate distribution space approximated by fat-free mass (FFM) is strongly linked to sprint performance. Creatine monohydrate is a widely used ergogenic aid known for increasing anaerobic performance and FFM and the phosphagenic system contributes most to a 15-s all-out sprint.

Objectives

The aim of the study was to analyze the influence of creatine supplementation of 15-s work, FFM, and ΔLa.

Methods

Twenty male and 5 female cyclists underwent a placebo-controlled, crossover design with 4 laboratory visits. After a familiarization trial, baseline measurements were performed. Placebo (4 × 5 g/d maltodextrin) and creatine monohydrate (4 × 5 g/d) were administered for 5 d before the respective trials. All participants underwent this order of trials and performed a 15-s all-out sprint test on a Cyclus2-ergometer. Capillary blood was sampled before and every minute (for 8 min) after the sprint to determine ΔLa. Body composition was determined employing bioelectric impedance analysis.

Results

Creatine supplementation significantly increased 15-s work output and FFM compared with baseline and placebo conditions. However, no significant differences were found in capillary blood lactate accumulation (ΔLa) or glycolytic contribution.

Conclusions

The results indicate potential differences in limitations of sprint performance of participants. Responders to creatine supplementation are potentially limited by mechanical or metabolic factors. The findings of this study highlight the importance of considering supplementation of creatine monohydrate when undergoing testing for the maximal glycolytic rate.

studies.title: Creatine supplementation does not enhance submaximal aerobic training adaptations in healthy young men and women.
studies.abstract: The benefits of dietary creatine supplementation on muscle performance are generally related to an increase in muscle phosphocreatine content. However, creatine supplementation may benefit endurance sports through increased glycogen re-synthesis following exercise. This study investigated the effect of creatine supplementation on muscle glycogen content, submaximal exercise fuel utilisation and endurance performance following 4 weeks of endurance training. Thirteen healthy, physically active, non-vegetarian subjects volunteered to take part and completed the study. Subjects were supplemented with either creatine monohydrate (CREAT, n = 7) or placebo-maltodextrin (CON, n = 6). Submaximal fuel utilisation and endurance performance were assessed before and after a 4 week endurance training program. Muscle biopsies were also collected before and following training for assessment of muscle creatine and glycogen content. Training increased quadriceps glycogen content to the same degree (approximately 20%) in both groups (P = 0.04). There was a significant training effect on submaximal fuel utilisation and improved endurance performance. However, there was no significant treatment effect of creatine supplementation. Creatine supplementation does not effect metabolic adaptations to endurance training.

explanation.what_it_is_line: A small amino acid derivative your body naturally makes; sold as powder to boost muscle and brain.
explanation.what_it_is: Creatine monohydrate is a compound made of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen (chemical formula C₄H₁₁N₃O₂·H₂O). Your body produces it naturally in the liver and kidneys, and it's also found in meat and fish. The supplement form is a white powder, usually mixed into water or a drink, delivering the same molecule your body already uses.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Supplies the energy currency your muscles need during intense effort; also appears to support brain energy and cell protection.
explanation.how_it_works: Creatine works by boosting ATP — the molecule cells burn for quick, intense energy. When you do a heavy lift or sprint, your muscles rapidly consume ATP. Creatine bonds to phosphate to form creatine phosphate, which acts as an energy reserve, donating a phosphate back to ATP to regenerate it faster than muscle can on its own. This is especially powerful in short, hard bursts of effort. Beyond muscle, creatine accumulates in the brain and may support energy there too; it also appears to reduce oxidative stress (cellular damage from reactive molecules) and may stabilize cell energy metabolism, which could explain cognitive benefits observed in studies.
explanation.safety_line: Well tolerated in most people; short-term side effects mild; long-term safety and specific populations largely untested.
explanation.safety_detail: Randomized trials and meta-analyses spanning multiple years report few adverse events — mainly mild gastrointestinal upset or weight gain from water retention. However, most trials are short-term (weeks to months), and sample sizes in safety reporting are often small. The compound has not been systematically tested in several important populations.
safety_bullets: Kidney disease or impaired kidney function: creatine is processed by the kidneys; no controlled trials in this population — unknown if supplementation worsens function.
Pregnancy and nursing: absent from all major trials; untested — recommendation is to avoid.
Children and adolescents: minimal data; skeletal maturity and long-term effects unknown.
Drug interactions with NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) or medications affecting kidney function: not formally studied — caution advised if taking these regularly.
explanation.chem_meaning: Creatine monohydrate is a relatively small, polar (water-attracting) molecule, which is why it dissolves readily in water and can be absorbed by the gut. The attached water molecule (monohydrate) is just the crystalline form — once ingested, it dissociates and behaves as free creatine in the body. Its small size and polarity allow it to cross cell membranes readily and accumulate in muscle and brain tissue.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses—including studies from 2024, 2021, 2020, and 2026—consistently show that creatine supplementation combined with resistance training increases strength gains. A pooled analysis across 51 human studies found a mean difference of 4.43 units (range 0.0 to 8.86) in strength measures. Five independent meta-analyses converge on this result, indicating robust replication. Studies span adults under 50 years old, older adults, and postmenopausal women.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 51 human studies with consistent findings across multiple independent syntheses, adequately powered sample sizes (~311+ verified participants in subset reporting), and replicated evidence across age groups and training contexts.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twenty-one human studies (plus 1 animal) show that creatine added to resistance training increases lean muscle mass. A pooled effect found a mean difference of 0.68 kg (range 0.26 to 1.11). Studies include a large meta-analysis of 1,192 participants examining age, sex, and exercise type; a regional hypertrophy study (n=44); and a systematic review of 1,542 participants. Seven independent meta-analyses converge on this outcome.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 21 human studies with consistent effects, seven replicated syntheses, and combined verified sample sizes over 2,870 participants across multiple study designs and populations.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twenty-two human studies plus 5 animal studies show creatine improves cognition or cognitive resilience. A 2023 meta-analysis examined memory effects in healthy individuals. A large 2026 systematic review (n=1,542) looked at cognition in older adults. A 2026 RCT found creatine reduced cognitive impairment from sleep deprivation. Five independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on cognitive benefits, with approximately 2,274 verified participants.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 22 human studies with consistent findings across ages and cognitive tasks (memory, sleep-deprivation resilience), five replicated syntheses, and a large combined sample size—though individual trial durations vary.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nineteen human studies examine endurance—including meta-analyses from 2023 (n=13 for one analysis), 2019 on soccer players, and RCTs in trained cyclists and children with muscular dystrophy. Studies measure VO₂, cycling performance, and sport-specific endurance. However, the meta-analyses present in the records do not report a pooled effect or clear consensus; findings vary by population and task.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects 19 human studies with inconsistent conclusions across contexts (benefit in some populations, no benefit in trained cyclists), no single pooled analysis confirming agreement, and variation by sport and fitness level—solid evidence that creatine *may* help endurance, but not consistently proven in all populations.

explanation.evidence_base: This is among the most studied supplements in humans. The evidence base is predominantly human (51–22 human studies per outcome) with multiple independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews published 2019–2026, indicating active, replicated research. Studies span diverse ages (young adults, aging, postmenopausal), training contexts (resistance, endurance, sport-specific), and cognitive tasks. Animal data is sparse and secondary. The convergence of five to seven independent syntheses per outcome (except endurance, which shows inconsistency) reflects well-established and repeatedly confirmed effects.
explanation.open_questions: The records show wide coverage in adults and older populations, but children and adolescents appear minimally studied—only one RCT (n=11) in children with muscular dystrophy is listed. Endurance is the least consistent outcome, with no unified pooled analysis across the retrieved trials; it is unclear whether benefit depends on training status, sport, or creatine loading protocol. Long-term studies (beyond 6–12 months) and effects in people with kidney disease, pregnancy, or concurrent use of NSAIDs or renal medications are absent from the records—these represent true unknowns rather than proven non-effects.

appraisal.headline: The evidence base is genuinely strong for muscle strength and growth, with multiple independent meta-analyses and adequate sample sizes; cognition claims rest on weaker ground, and the endurance outcome lacks pooled effect estimates and shows acknowledged inconsistency.

concerns.issue: Cognition outcome lacks pooled effect size
concerns.detail: Unlike strength and growth (which report mean differences with confidence intervals), the cognition outcome explicitly states 'pooled effect: none extractable.' This means the 5 meta-analyses/systematic reviews that 'converge' on the outcome did not themselves synthesize a unified effect estimate—convergence may mean they all found mixed or null results, not a consistent benefit. The reader cannot distinguish between 'creatine helps cognition' and 'studies agree the effect is heterogeneous or absent.'

concerns.issue: Endurance outcome shows acknowledged inconsistency without resolution
concerns.detail: The engine explicitly notes 'Inconsistency: several studies exist but no pooled analysis confirms they agree; held at moderate pending review.' Three meta-analyses are listed, yet no pooled effect is reported. This suggests the meta-analyses either disagreed or found heterogeneity the engine deemed unresolved. A 'Moderate' grade on an outcome with unresolved inconsistency is a red flag—the true effect may be null, small, or population-dependent.

concerns.issue: Majority of individual studies lack reported sample sizes
concerns.detail: Across all outcomes, 13–28 of 19–54 studies do not report sample size in the abstracts provided. While the engine notes 'true total is substantially larger,' this opacity creates hidden heterogeneity in the evidence base. Small unpublished studies may cluster in certain subdomains (e.g., cognition), skewing the apparent effect. The precision calculation rests on only 7–13 of 22–54 studies; the unlisted studies could systematically differ in quality or effect direction.

concerns.issue: Strength and growth outcomes conflate resistance training with creatine
concerns.detail: Most included trials (42 of 51 for strength; 14 of 21 for growth) are RCTs, but nearly all combine creatine supplementation with resistance training. The pooled effects (mean_diff 4.43 for strength, 0.68 for growth) cannot isolate creatine's contribution from the exercise effect. Without active control arms testing creatine alone vs. training alone, the evidence addresses 'creatine + training' not 'creatine' in isolation. Readers may overestimate creatine's independent potency.

For strength and growth, roughly 50% of the abstracts are from 2024–2026 (current year), whereas older studies (1997–2010) are sparse in the provided records. This temporal clustering raises the possibility of (a) selective retrieval favoring recent papers, (b) publication bias toward positive recent findings, or (c) true recent expansion of the field. Without year-by-year sample counts, it is unclear whether the 'Strong' grades reflect a long-standing consensus or a recent wave of studies, some of which may not yet be validated by independent replication.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Creatine's mechanism—replenishing ATP in muscle via phosphocreatine and potentially increasing intracellular water/glycogen in myocytes—plausibly supports muscle strength and hypertrophy gains. The mechanism directly targets the energy substrate and osmotic milieu of contraction, so the link to resistance-training outcomes is mechanistically sound. However, the cognition claim is a larger inferential leap: creatine's benefit for brain phosphocreatine recycling is theoretically plausible (especially in vegetarians with lower baseline creatine), but cognition depends on numerous distributed systems; the recorded studies do not extract a pooled effect, suggesting heterogeneous mechanisms or null results in individual trials. The gap between 'phosphocreatine availability in neurons' and 'measurable cognition in healthy adults' is not trivially bridged by the current evidence.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptical expert would note that the strength and growth grades conflate training stimulus with supplementation—most trials lack a creatine-only arm or proper dose-response design, so the pooled effect sizes reflect additive benefit of exercise, not creatine's independent contribution. For cognition, the absence of a reportable pooled effect despite 'convergence' of 5 systematic reviews is a smoke signal; convergence likely means studies disagree or show small/null effects, and the outcome should not be graded 'Strong.' For endurance, the engine's own assessment ('unresolved inconsistency') contradicts a 'Moderate' grade. Taken together, the 'Strong' tier inflates confidence: strength and growth are moderately well-supported under the assumption that creatine + training is the claimed intervention, but cognition and endurance lack credible synthesis.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: For strength/growth: a set of RCTs comparing creatine alone, training alone, combined, and placebo + training in parallel, with pre-registered cognitive/endurance secondary outcomes. For cognition: a new meta-analysis that attempts to pool effect sizes from the 14 RCTs, with explicit heterogeneity assessment and subgroup analysis by population (vegetarians, older adults, sleep-deprived), resolving whether any subgroup shows benefit. For endurance: a single large, adequately-powered RCT in a high-responder population (e.g., trained cyclists) with VO₂max and time-trial outcomes, to settle whether creatine + training improves aerobic capacity or only strength-endurance.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un pequeño derivado de aminoácido que tu cuerpo produce naturalmente; se vende en polvo para potenciar músculo y cerebro.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La creatina monohidratada es un compuesto hecho de carbono, hidrógeno, nitrógeno y oxígeno (fórmula química C₄H₁₁N₃O₂·H₂O). Tu cuerpo la produce naturalmente en el hígado y los riñones, y también se encuentra en la carne y el pescado. La forma de suplemento es un polvo blanco, generalmente mezclado en agua o una bebida, que aporta la misma molécula que tu cuerpo ya utiliza.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Suministra la moneda energética que tus músculos necesitan durante esfuerzo intenso; también parece apoyar la energía cerebral y la protección celular.
explanation_es.how_it_works: La creatina funciona al potenciar el ATP, la molécula que las células queman para obtener energía rápida e intensa. Cuando haces un levantamiento pesado o un sprint, tus músculos consumen rápidamente ATP. La creatina se une al fosfato para formar fosfato de creatina, que actúa como una reserva de energía, donando un fosfato de vuelta al ATP para regenerarlo más rápidamente de lo que el músculo puede hacerlo por sí solo. Esto es especialmente poderoso en ráfagas cortas de esfuerzo intenso. Más allá del músculo, la creatina se acumula en el cerebro y puede apoyar la energía allí también; también parece reducir el estrés oxidativo (daño celular de moléculas reactivas) y puede estabilizar el metabolismo energético celular, lo que podría explicar los beneficios cognitivos observados en estudios.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerada en la mayoría de las personas; los efectos secundarios a corto plazo son leves; la seguridad a largo plazo y en poblaciones específicas está largamente sin probar.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos aleatorizados y metanálisis que abarcan varios años reportan pocos eventos adversos, principalmente molestias gastrointestinales leves o aumento de peso por retención de agua. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los ensayos son a corto plazo (semanas a meses), y los tamaños de muestra en reportes de seguridad suelen ser pequeños. El compuesto no ha sido probado sistemáticamente en varias poblaciones importantes.
safety_bullets: Enfermedad renal o función renal deteriorada: la creatina es procesada por los riñones; no hay ensayos controlados en esta población — se desconoce si la suplementación empeora la función.
Embarazo y lactancia: ausente de todos los ensayos principales; sin probar — la recomendación es evitarla.
Niños y adolescentes: datos mínimos; la madurez esquelética y los efectos a largo plazo son desconocidos.
Interacciones medicamentosas con AINEs (p. ej., ibuprofeno) o medicamentos que afecten la función renal: no se han estudiado formalmente — se aconseja precaución si se toman regularmente.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La creatina monohidratada es una molécula relativamente pequeña y polar (que atrae agua), razón por la cual se disuelve fácilmente en agua y puede ser absorbida por el intestino. La molécula de agua adjunta (monohidratada) es simplemente la forma cristalina — una vez ingerida, se disocia y se comporta como creatina libre en el cuerpo. Su tamaño pequeño y polaridad le permiten cruzar las membranas celulares fácilmente y acumularse en el tejido muscular y cerebral.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Múltiples revisiones sistemáticas y metanálisis—incluyendo estudios de 2024, 2021, 2020 y 2026—muestran consistentemente que la suplementación de creatina combinada con entrenamiento de resistencia aumenta las ganancias de fuerza. Un análisis agrupado en 51 estudios humanos encontró una diferencia media de 4,43 unidades (rango 0,0 a 8,86) en medidas de fuerza. Cinco metanálisis independientes convergen en este resultado, indicando replicación robusta. Los estudios abarcan adultos menores de 50 años, adultos mayores y mujeres posmenopáusicas.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Fuerte refleja 51 estudios humanos con hallazgos consistentes en múltiples síntesis independientes, tamaños de muestra adecuadamente potenciados (~311+ participantes verificados en reportes de subconjuntos), y evidencia replicada en grupos de edad y contextos de entrenamiento.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Veintiún estudios humanos (más 1 animal) muestran que la creatina añadida al entrenamiento de resistencia aumenta la masa muscular magra. Un efecto agrupado encontró una diferencia media de 0,68 kg (rango 0,26 a 1,11). Los estudios incluyen un gran metanálisis de 1.192 participantes examinando edad, sexo y tipo de ejercicio; un estudio de hipertrofia regional (n=44); y una revisión sistemática de 1.542 participantes. Siete metanálisis independientes convergen en este resultado.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Fuerte refleja 21 estudios humanos con efectos consistentes, siete síntesis replicadas, y tamaños de muestra verificados combinados superiores a 2.870 participantes en múltiples diseños de estudio y poblaciones.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Veintidós estudios humanos más 5 estudios animales muestran que la creatina mejora la cognición o la resiliencia cognitiva. Un metanálisis de 2023 examinó efectos de memoria en individuos sanos. Una gran revisión sistemática de 2026 (n=1.542) examinó cognición en adultos mayores. Un ensayo controlado aleatorio de 2026 encontró que la creatina redujo el deterioro cognitivo por privación de sueño. Cinco metanálisis y revisiones sistemáticas independientes convergen en beneficios cognitivos, con aproximadamente 2.274 participantes verificados.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Fuerte refleja 22 estudios humanos con hallazgos consistentes en edades y tareas cognitivas (memoria, resiliencia ante privación de sueño), cinco síntesis replicadas, y un tamaño de muestra combinado grande—aunque las duraciones de los ensayos individuales varían.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Diecinueve estudios humanos examinan resistencia—incluyendo metanálisis de 2023 (n=13 para un análisis), 2019 sobre jugadores de fútbol, y ensayos controlados aleatorizados en ciclistas entrenados y niños con distrofia muscular. Los estudios miden VO₂, rendimiento en ciclismo y resistencia específica del deporte. Sin embargo, los metanálisis presentes en los registros no reportan un efecto agrupado o consenso claro; los hallazgos varían por población y tarea.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Moderada refleja 19 estudios humanos con conclusiones inconsistentes en diferentes contextos (beneficio en algunas poblaciones, sin beneficio en ciclistas entrenados), sin un solo análisis agrupado que confirme acuerdo, y variación por deporte y nivel de fitness—evidencia sólida de que la creatina *podría* ayudar en resistencia, pero no probado consistentemente en todas las poblaciones.

explanation_es.evidence_base: Este es uno de los suplementos más estudiados en humanos. La base de evidencia es predominantemente humana (51–22 estudios humanos por resultado) con múltiples metanálisis y revisiones sistemáticas independientes publicadas 2019–2026, indicando investigación activa y replicada. Los estudios abarcan edades diversas (adultos jóvenes, envejecimiento, posmenopáusicas), contextos de entrenamiento (resistencia, resistencia, específicos del deporte) y tareas cognitivas. Los datos animales son escasos y secundarios. La convergencia de cinco a siete síntesis independientes por resultado (excepto resistencia, que muestra inconsistencia) refleja efectos bien establecidos y repetidamente confirmados.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros muestran cobertura amplia en poblaciones adultas y mayores, pero niños y adolescentes parecen estar minimamente estudiados—solo se lista un ensayo controlado aleatorio (n=11) en niños con distrofia muscular. La resistencia es el resultado menos consistente, sin un análisis agrupado unificado en los ensayos recuperados; no está claro si el beneficio depende del estado de entrenamiento, del deporte o del protocolo de carga de creatina. Los estudios a largo plazo (más allá de 6–12 meses) y los efectos en personas con enfermedad renal, embarazo o uso concurrente de AINEs o medicamentos renales están ausentes de los registros—estos representan verdaderas incógnitas en lugar de no efectos probados.

appraisal_es.headline: La base de evidencia es genuinamente sólida para la fuerza muscular y el crecimiento, con múltiples metanálisis independientes y tamaños de muestra adecuados; las afirmaciones sobre cognición descansan en bases más débiles, y el resultado de resistencia carece de estimaciones de efectos agrupados y muestra inconsistencia reconocida.

concerns.issue: El resultado de cognición carece de tamaño de efecto agrupado
concerns.detail: A diferencia de fuerza y crecimiento (que reportan diferencias medias con intervalos de confianza), el resultado de cognición explícitamente establece 'efecto agrupado: ninguno extraíble.' Esto significa que los 5 metanálisis/revisiones sistemáticas que 'convergen' en el resultado no sintetizaron en sí mismos una estimación de efecto unificada—la convergencia puede significar que todos encontraron resultados mixtos o nulos, no un beneficio consistente. El lector no puede distinguir entre 'la creatina ayuda la cognición' y 'los estudios están de acuerdo en que el efecto es heterogéneo o ausente.'

concerns.issue: El resultado de resistencia muestra inconsistencia reconocida sin resolución
concerns.detail: El motor explícitamente señala 'Inconsistencia: varios estudios existen pero ningún análisis agrupado confirma que estén de acuerdo; mantenido en moderado pendiente de revisión.' Se enumeran tres metanálisis, pero no se reporta efecto agrupado. Esto sugiere que los metanálisis o bien estuvieron en desacuerdo o encontraron heterogeneidad que el motor consideró sin resolver. Una calificación 'Moderada' en un resultado con inconsistencia sin resolver es una señal de alerta—el efecto verdadero puede ser nulo, pequeño, o dependiente de la población.

concerns.issue: La mayoría de estudios individuales no reportan tamaños de muestra
concerns.detail: Entre todos los resultados, 13–28 de 19–54 estudios no reportan tamaño de muestra en los resúmenes proporcionados. Aunque el motor señala 'el total verdadero es sustancialmente mayor,' esta opacidad crea heterogeneidad oculta en la base de evidencia. Estudios pequeños no publicados pueden agruparse en ciertos subdominios (p. ej., cognición), sesgando el efecto aparente. El cálculo de precisión descansa en solo 7–13 de 22–54 estudios; los estudios no listados podrían diferir sistemáticamente en calidad o dirección del efecto.

concerns.issue: Los resultados de fuerza y crecimiento confunden el entrenamiento de resistencia con la creatina
concerns.detail: La mayoría de ensayos incluidos (42 de 51 para fuerza; 14 de 21 para crecimiento) son ECA, pero casi todos combinan suplementación de creatina con entrenamiento de resistencia. Los efectos agrupados (diferencia_media 4.43 para fuerza, 0.68 para crecimiento) no pueden aislar la contribución de la creatina del efecto del ejercicio. Sin brazos de control activo que prueben creatina sola vs. entrenamiento solo, la evidencia aborda 'creatina + entrenamiento' no 'creatina' en aislamiento. Los lectores pueden sobrestimar la potencia independiente de la creatina.

Para fuerza y crecimiento, aproximadamente el 50% de los resúmenes son de 2024–2026 (año actual), mientras que estudios más antiguos (1997–2010) son escasos en los registros proporcionados. Este agrupamiento temporal plantea la posibilidad de (a) recuperación selectiva favoreciendo artículos recientes, (b) sesgo de publicación hacia hallazgos recientes positivos, o (c) expansión real reciente del campo. Sin recuentos de muestra año por año, es incierto si las calificaciones 'Sólidas' reflejan un consenso duradero o una ola reciente de estudios, algunos de los cuales podrían aún no ser validados por replicación independiente.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo de la creatina—reponiendo ATP en músculo vía fosfocreatina y potencialmente aumentando agua intracelular/glucógeno en miocitos—plausiblemente apoya ganancias de fuerza y hipertrofia muscular. El mecanismo apunta directamente al sustrato energético y medio osmótico de la contracción, así que el vínculo a resultados de entrenamiento de resistencia es mecanísticamente sólido. Sin embargo, la afirmación de cognición es un salto inferencial mayor: el beneficio de la creatina para el reciclaje de fosfocreatina cerebral es teóricamente plausible (especialmente en vegetarianos con creatina basal más baja), pero la cognición depende de numerosos sistemas distribuidos; los estudios registrados no extraen un efecto agrupado, sugiriendo mecanismos heterogéneos o resultados nulos en ensayos individuales. La brecha entre 'disponibilidad de fosfocreatina en neuronas' y 'cognición medible en adultos sanos' no es trivialmente cerrada por la evidencia actual.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un experto escéptico señalaría que las calificaciones de fuerza y crecimiento confunden estímulo de entrenamiento con suplementación—la mayoría de ensayos carecen de un brazo solo creatina o diseño de dosis-respuesta adecuado, así que los tamaños de efecto agrupados reflejan beneficio aditivo del ejercicio, no la contribución independiente de la creatina. Para cognición, la ausencia de un efecto reportable agrupado a pesar de 'convergencia' de 5 revisiones sistemáticas es una señal de humo; la convergencia probablemente significa que los estudios estén en desacuerdo o muestren efectos pequeños/nulos, y el resultado no debería ser calificado 'Sólido.' Para resistencia, la propia evaluación del motor ('inconsistencia sin resolver') contradice una calificación 'Moderada.' En conjunto, el nivel 'Sólido' infla la confianza: fuerza y crecimiento están moderadamente bien apoyados bajo el supuesto de que creatina + entrenamiento es la intervención reclamada, pero cognición y resistencia carecen de síntesis creíble.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Para fuerza/crecimiento: un conjunto de ECA comparando creatina sola, entrenamiento solo, combinado, y placebo + entrenamiento en paralelo, con resultados secundarios cognitivos/de resistencia preregistrados. Para cognición: un nuevo metanálisis que intente agrupar tamaños de efecto de los 14 ECA, con evaluación explícita de heterogeneidad y análisis de subgrupos por población (vegetarianos, adultos mayores, privados de sueño), resolviendo si algún subgrupo muestra beneficio. Para resistencia: un único ECA grande, adecuadamente potenciado, en una población respondedora alta (p. ej., ciclistas entrenados) con resultados de VO₂máx y prueba de tiempo, para resolver si creatina + entrenamiento mejora la capacidad aeróbica o solo la resistencia-fuerza.
